title: US Pushes Nationwide Arms Embargo on Sudan as Washington Prepares Largest Visa Revocation in History
subhead: Washington escalates on two fronts: a UN Security Council push to expand Sudan's arms embargo nationwide, and a plan to revoke up to 200,000 visas from asylum-seekers. Meanwhile the US-Canada trade war deepens and new Iran sanctions target third countries.

sections.heading: US Moves to Expand Sudan Arms Embargo Nationwide
sections.body:
The United States is pressing the UN Security Council to expand Sudan's arms embargo from Darfur to the entire country, in a bid to choke off the external support that has sustained a war now in its fourth year. Trump's senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, told the Security Council on Monday that financial, military and political backing for both the government forces and the rival Rapid Support Forces remains a driver of the conflict, which has killed at least 59,000 people and displaced some 13 million, according to AP.

The proposed US resolution would apply the embargo to all parties operating in Sudan's territory and explicitly reaffirm that drones and related technologies fall under it. Boulos did not name the countries providing support, but AP notes Egypt has backed the military while UN experts and human rights groups have accused the UAE of arming the RSF, a charge Abu Dhabi denies.
sections.whyItMatters: A nationwide embargo would be the first real attempt to cut the external arms flows that have kept Sudan's war grinding on, and it tests whether Washington can rally the Security Council on an African crisis while its attention is fixed on Iran.

sections.heading: Washington Prepares Largest Mass Visa Revocation in US History
sections.body:
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the United States, according to State Department documents obtained by AP and two US officials. The move, coordinated with the Department of Homeland Security, would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott confirmed the coordination, saying the department is identifying and revoking the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who came as short-term visitors but then filed for asylum. He declined to give a number, calling the process ongoing and rolling. Officials said most of those with pending asylum cases would be recategorized but would lose their business or tourism status, though the revocations would not necessarily mean immediate deportation.
sections.whyItMatters: If it proceeds, the revocation would mark a sharp escalation of the administration's immigration crackdown, targeting people already inside the US system and setting up a major legal and diplomatic confrontation over asylum policy.

sections.heading: US-Canada Trade War Deepens as Retaliation Set for September
sections.body:
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products early Saturday, and Canada said it would retaliate beginning September 8 after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain between the historic allies, AP reports. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada's response on Parliament Hill, while President Donald Trump told Canadian leaders to 'fall in line.'

The escalation follows the collapse of talks that had been meant to head off a new round of tariffs. The dispute now carries real economic weight on both sides of the border, hitting steel and other industrial goods at a moment when supply chains are already under strain.
sections.whyItMatters: A full-blown tariff war between the US and its largest trading partner would ripple through North American manufacturing and energy trade, and it signals that Washington is willing to pressure even its closest allies as part of its broader trade posture.

sections.heading: New Iran Sanctions Target Third Countries as Rial Collapses
sections.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new sanctions on Monday aimed at blocking all potential sources of revenue for Iran, including secondary sanctions on countries that continue to do business with Tehran, according to AP. The Iranian rial dropped to 2.02 million to the dollar as trading opened, extending a slide that began well before the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

Iran warned of a harsh response to the new measures. In a sign of Tehran's diplomatic maneuvering, Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf met Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Gen. Asim Munir in Tehran on Monday. The secondary sanctions are the sharpest escalation yet of Washington's economic campaign, threatening to force third countries to choose between the US financial system and trade with Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: Secondary sanctions raise the cost of doing business with Iran for every country, not just Tehran, and could reshape trade and energy relationships across the Gulf and South Asia even as the military standoff over Hormuz continues.

sections.heading: West Bank Violence Draws Arrest of Teenage Settler
sections.body:
Israeli police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in connection with the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian man with a pipe in the occupied West Bank, AP reports. The arrest comes amid a broader pattern of settler violence that has drawn international criticism and added friction to US-Israel relations.

The incident is a reminder that the West Bank remains a live flashpoint even as attention focuses on Gaza and the wider Iran confrontation, with settler attacks and Palestinian casualties continuing to feed instability in the territory.
sections.whyItMatters: Settler violence in the West Bank is a persistent driver of regional instability and a recurring point of tension between Washington and Jerusalem, with the potential to ignite broader confrontations at any time.

bottomLine: Today's developments show Washington escalating on multiple fronts at once: a UN push to expand Sudan's arms embargo nationwide, the largest mass visa revocation in US history, a deepening tariff war with Canada, and new secondary sanctions on Iran that force third countries to pick a side. The common thread is an administration willing to use economic and legal leverage aggressively against adversaries and allies alike. The Iran sanctions and the Sudan embargo both aim to cut external support to hostile actors, while the visa and tariff moves signal a harder line on immigration and trade. The risk is that these parallel confrontations compound each other, stretching US attention and diplomatic capital across the Middle East, Africa, and North America simultaneously.
